subsection: 9. Northern Ireland during World War II and case study: Belfast during World War II

notes.h: Northern Ireland at war: unionism, neutrality and conscription
notes.b: Northern Ireland was part of the United Kingdom, so it went to war with Britain, while the South stayed neutral. That contrast shaped how unionists and nationalists in the North each saw the war.
points: Under the Government of Ireland Act (1920), Northern Ireland was a self-governing part of the United Kingdom with a Unionist government at Stormont since 1921, a Protestant majority and a Catholic nationalist minority. This is the background to every wartime division.

The United Kingdom declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, so Northern Ireland was at war from that day. Unionists contrasted its loyalty with the South's neutrality (the South's policy of the 'Emergency', staying out of the war).

Ulster Unionism, the political tradition defending Northern Ireland's place in the United Kingdom, presented the war effort as proof of the region's British loyalty. This strengthened the unionist case against a united Ireland, because the South had stayed out.

Nationalists in the North (those who wanted a united Ireland) were divided. Many Catholics volunteered for the forces, while others resented unionist rule and would not back a war effort run by a government they felt excluded them.
Conscription (compulsory military service) was introduced in Britain in 1939 but not applied to Northern Ireland. This meant that enlistment from the North, Catholic and Protestant, was voluntary.

In May 1941 the British government announced, then abandoned, a plan to extend conscription to Northern Ireland. Nationalists, the Catholic bishops (for example Cardinal MacRory of Armagh) and the Dublin government protested, although unionist ministers had favoured extension.

The IRA (the Irish Republican Army, a group that used force against partition) was active in Belfast. Tom Williams, an IRA member aged 19, was hanged at Crumlin Road Gaol on 2 September 1942 for killing a policeman during an IRA operation in April 1942.
The execution of Tom Williams deepened nationalist resentment, because it confirmed for many nationalists that the state treated them as enemies rather than as citizens.
notes.tip: In a North and South comparison, keep the Northern points distinct: Northern Ireland was at war from September 1939, the South neutral. Give at least three specific, dated points for each side.

notes.b: Northern Ireland changed prime minister in the middle of the war. The change came from a death, then from a loss of confidence in the man who replaced him.
points: James Craig (Lord Craigavon), the long-serving Prime Minister, died on 24 November 1940. John Miller Andrews succeeded him as Prime Minister in late November 1940.
Andrews was criticised for an elderly cabinet and for a slow response to the Blitz (the German bombing of British cities). This made his government look unfit to lead a region at war.

Andrews resigned in April 1943 after a revolt by younger ministers and backbenchers over his leadership. Criticism over preparation for air attack was one strand in the discontent that ended his premiership, not the only cause.
Basil Brooke became Prime Minister in April 1943 and led the government until 1963. Do not confuse the three leaders: Craig (died November 1940), Andrews (1940 to 1943) and Brooke (1943 to 1963).
Brooke was an energetic unionist. He had been Minister of Agriculture (1933 to 1941) and then Minister of Commerce and Production, so he was well placed to push war production and farming.
notes.tip: Examiners expect you to keep Craig, Andrews and Brooke and their dates apart. If asked about Andrews's fall, give several strands of criticism (age, slowness, the Blitz response) rather than one flat cause.

notes.h: Industry, agriculture and employment in wartime
notes.b: The war brought full employment to a region that had suffered mass unemployment since the 1920s. Belfast's heavy industries were exactly what a country at war needed.
points: In the 1930s the Depression hit Northern Ireland's export industries, shipbuilding and linen, and left heavy unemployment. War orders reversed this.
Harland and Wolff, on Queen's Island in Belfast, built warships and merchant ships and repaired many vessels for the Admiralty (the British navy's governing department).
Short Brothers (Short and Harland) built Stirling bombers and other aircraft in Belfast, which made the aircraft factory a vital war industry.
Engineering firms made munitions and other war equipment. The rope works and linen mills made parachutes, tents, uniforms and rope, so even a traditional peacetime industry was turned to war needs.
Farmers were ordered to plough more land under compulsory tillage orders, which raised the acreage under crops. Northern Ireland became an important food supplier to Britain.
Unemployment fell sharply as war contracts came in, women entered factories in large numbers, and wages rose.
Industrial unrest still occurred over pay and conditions in the shipyards and engineering works, despite full employment, because workers pressed for a share of the profits from war production.
The Northern Ireland government worked closely with Whitehall (the British government's ministries in London), including the Ministry of Aircraft Production and the Admiralty.
notes.tip: For a paragraph on Northern Ireland at war, name Harland and Wolff, Short Brothers, linen and farming, and state full employment. Each correct, specific fact earns marks.

notes.h: Case study background: why Belfast was a target and why it was unprepared
notes.b: Belfast's industries made it a natural target, yet the government and city were badly prepared for air attack. This mismatch explains the scale of the damage in 1941.
points: Germany's conquest of France in 1940 brought Belfast within range of German bombers, and the Blitz on British cities began in 1940.
Belfast was an obvious target because of the shipyard, the aircraft factory, the docks and the engineering works, all producing for the war effort.
The Northern government assumed that Belfast was out of range of German airfields. This assumption of safety is the main reason preparations were weak.
Before April 1941 the city had few public air-raid shelters, and many working-class houses had no shelter at all, so people had nowhere safe to go when the bombers came.
Anti-aircraft defences were small: the city had only a handful of heavy guns, and no night-fighter squadrons were based in Northern Ireland in April 1941.
A German reconnaissance flight photographed Belfast in late 1940 and showed that the city was within reach, but the government did not accelerate preparations.
Fire services were small and under-equipped, so the authorities depended on outside help once the fires began.
Overcrowded slum housing near the docks and mills increased the risk of casualties and fire, because bombs and flames spread quickly through tightly packed terraces.
notes.tip: If asked why Belfast was unprepared, list the assumption of safety, few shelters, small anti-aircraft defences, no night fighters and a small fire service.

notes.h: The Belfast Blitz, April and May 1941
notes.b: Three raids in spring 1941 devastated Belfast. Keep them apart by date and scale: a small raid in early April, the Easter Tuesday raid, and the May incendiary attack.
points: The raid of 7-8 April 1941 was smaller and aimed at the shipyard. About a dozen people were killed.
The main raid was on the night of 15-16 April 1941, Easter Tuesday (15 April), when about 180 German bombers attacked the city.
About 900 people were killed on Easter Tuesday, and the working-class districts of north and east Belfast were worst hit. It was the deadliest night of the Blitz outside London.
The raid of 4-5 May 1941 was an incendiary attack (using bombs that start fires) on the shipyard, the aircraft factory and the docks. About 150 people were killed.
In all the Blitz killed about 1,000 people and damaged more than half of the city's houses. Do not give a larger total.
Tens of thousands of people were left homeless, because so much of the housing had been destroyed or made unsafe.
notes.tip: A 40-mark paragraph on the Blitz earns marks for each correct dated fact: the April and May raids, the main raid's date, about 180 bombers, about 900 dead, the damage, the ditchers and the help from Dublin. A short answer may ask for the figure killed, or what the raids showed: that Northern Ireland was not safe.

notes.h: Living with the Blitz: ditchers, help from Dublin and the dead
notes.b: The raids overwhelmed the city's ability to cope. People fled, help came across the border from a neutral state, and the authorities struggled to deal with the dead.
points: After the raids, tens of thousands of people left the city each night to sleep in the countryside. They were known as ditchers, because they often slept in fields and ditches, and returned to work by day.
On the night of 15-16 April, fire brigades from Dublin, Dun Laoghaire, Dundalk and Drogheda crossed the border to help, with de Valera's authorisation.
This help was significant because it came from a neutral state: the South was not at war, yet it sent firefighters into the United Kingdom to save a city in the North.
Public buildings served as temporary mortuaries, among them the Falls Road baths, because the city mortuaries were overwhelmed by the number of dead.
notes.tip: Short answers often ask which government helped (Dublin) or what the raids showed. Say that fire brigades crossed the border from the neutral South with de Valera's authorisation.

notes.h: Aftermath: evacuation and what it revealed
notes.b: The raids showed up the city's poverty and the weakness of its public services. The treatment of the evacuees (people moved out of danger) and the criticism of the government were the political consequences.
points: Children and mothers were evacuated to country areas, and many people took refuge in barns and church halls. Churches, schools and halls in towns near Belfast took in refugees, and the authorities opened emergency rest centres.
Host families in rural areas were shocked by the poor health, clothing and hygiene of some evacuees from the slums, because they had not met such poverty before.
The condition of the children became a theme in debates on housing and public health, as it had in Britain in 1939, and strengthened the argument that the state should improve slum housing.
Many evacuees drifted back to Belfast within weeks, and housing remained scarce for years.
The Unionist government was criticised for its slow response and its poor preparation. This was one strand in the discontent that ended Andrews's premiership in 1943.
notes.tip: Source questions on evacuees ask you to compare two writers (sympathy versus blame), say what a source leaves out (no statistics) and judge how objective it is. Link the evacuees' poverty to housing and public health.

notes.h: American troops and the wartime city
notes.b: From 1942 Northern Ireland became a staging area for the Allied build-up (the gathering of troops and supplies for the invasion of Europe). The American presence changed daily life.
points: The first American troops landed at Dufferin Quay, Belfast, on 26 January 1942.
By 1944 there were over 100,000 American servicemen in Northern Ireland, in camps, airfields and ports.
They brought money, goods unavailable in rationed Britain and a new popular culture, including dances and cinema, so their presence was felt widely in everyday life.
US units were segregated, with Black American soldiers serving in separate units from white soldiers.

Northern Ireland's ports and airfields supported the Atlantic convoy escort (the protection of merchant ships crossing the Atlantic) and the preparation for D-Day, the Allied invasion of France in 1944.
notes.tip: For a paragraph on Northern Ireland at war, include the date and place of the first American landing (26 January 1942, Dufferin Quay) and the figure of over 100,000 by 1944.

notes.h: Social and political effects: housing, welfare and Labour
notes.b: The war raised expectations that the state should provide better housing, health and employment. Northern Ireland followed Britain in welfare reform, but its political structure stayed the same.
points: The destruction of housing made housing an urgent political issue after the war.

The Beveridge Report of 1942, a British plan for a post-war welfare state, shaped discussion of better health, housing and employment. Northern Ireland followed British welfare legislation under the policy of parity.
In February 1943 Jack Beattie, a Labour candidate, won the Belfast West by-election at Westminster, a sign of working-class discontent with the Unionist government.
Labour support rose, but the Unionist Party kept power at Stormont.

The Education Act (Northern Ireland) 1947 and the Health Services Act (Northern Ireland) 1948 came out of the wartime reform climate, which is how the war led to the origins of the welfare state in the North.
Sectarian divisions remained, and the Unionist government made no changes to the electoral system or policing.
notes.tip: Remember the paired judgement examiners reward: stronger British links and welfare reform against unchanged Unionist control.

notes.b: The war changed Belfast's economy and housing but not its religious division. This comparison is the core of the most common essay question.
points: Unemployment, high in 1939, was low in 1945 because of war contracts.
Large areas of housing had been destroyed or damaged, and many families lived in temporary housing.
Industries such as shipbuilding and aircraft were running at full capacity, but depended on wartime orders, so their future was uncertain once the orders stopped.
The Unionist Party was still in control, though challenged by Labour and criticised for the failures of civil defence.
The links with Britain were stronger, because of wartime co-operation and the promise of welfare reform.
Catholic and Protestant communities remained separate, and the border and the division from the South were more entrenched.
notes.tip: The commonest Higher essay asks how far Belfast in 1945 differed from 1939. Give a clear judgement (economy and housing changed, politics and religious division did not), supported by paired dated points such as full employment against the Blitz damage.

notes.h: Assessment: the war's effects on Northern Ireland
notes.b: Judgements depend on whether economic and social change or political continuity is stressed. Good answers weigh both and reach a conclusion.
points: Achievement: war production ended mass unemployment and brought full employment and better wages for many workers.
Achievement: the war strengthened Northern Ireland's place in the United Kingdom and prepared it to take part in the post-war welfare state.
Limit: the Blitz exposed poor preparation and housing, and the government had to answer for it.
Limit: the Unionist Party's control and the exclusion of the Catholic minority were unchanged, and sectarian division and the border were entrenched.
Contemporary view: unionists praised Northern Ireland's contribution to the war, while nationalists were critical of both the war role and the unionist government.

Overall: the war brought economic and social change but political continuity. Brian Barton is the main historian of the subject, with accounts of the Blitz (1989) and of Northern Ireland in the Second World War (1995).
notes.tip: Reach a clear judgement: economy and housing changed, politics and religious division did not. Support it with paired points, such as full employment against Blitz damage, and stronger British links against unchanged Unionist control.

keyTerms.definition: Seen from the North, the South's neutrality set Ireland apart from the British war effort and strengthened unionist arguments against unity.
The loyalist political tradition that presented the war effort as proof of Northern Ireland's British identity.
The German air raids on Belfast in April and May 1941, which killed about 1,000 people.
People who left Belfast at night after the raids to sleep in the countryside.
The removal of children and mothers from Belfast to rural areas after the raids.
The Belfast shipyard that built and repaired warships and merchant ships.
The 1942 British report proposing a welfare state, which shaped post-war reform in Northern Ireland.
The wartime Unionist governments, led by John Miller Andrews (1940–43) and Basil Brooke (1943–63).
